content: Urinary retention refers to the inability to pass urine despite persistent effort. Dysuria is characterized by a burning sensation or discomfort during urination. These symptoms may occur immediately after emptying the bladder. Patients often report a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying, a need to immediately attempt to void again, and post-micturition dribbling or leakage. In a large European study (EPIC) conducted across five countries, the prevalence of voiding symptoms among women was reported to be 19.5% (Irwin, 2006). Another study found that voiding difficulties were present in 7.2% to 12.8% of female urology patients visiting clinics (Choi, 2013). A survey of 15,861 women aged over 40 years in the US, UK, and Sweden revealed that terminal dribbling was the most common symptom (38.3%), followed by a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying (27.4%) and a weak urinary stream (20.1%) (Coyne, 2009a). While voiding dysfunction has been extensively studied in men, it is considered more complex in women. Female voiding dysfunction is poorly understood, challenging to treat, and lacks consensus on its standard definition, diagnosis, and management (Kupelian, 2006; Olujide, 2005). Voiding disorders in women are common but often remain untreated until they present with severe symptoms such as urinary retention, renal insufficiency, recurrent urinary tract infections, or overflow incontinence, particularly in cases of bladder outlet obstruction (Hajebrahimi, 2011; Olujide, 2005). Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) negatively impact various aspects of health-related quality of life, including general health perception, mental health, and overall bladder function. Women with voiding dysfunction often experience significant psychological and social burdens, with higher rates of depression and anxiety compared to asymptomatic individuals. These symptoms are more pronounced in women than in men (Fan, 2008; Kupelian, 2006). Voiding dysfunction symptoms often coexist with storage symptoms such as frequency, urgency, and nocturia, complicating diagnosis and management. Post-micturition symptoms are commonly associated with voiding dysfunction, and women may also report concurrent stress and urgency urinary incontinence (Robinson, 2012; Vella, 2012). Voiding dysfunction is linked to aging and pelvic organ prolapse. A history of hysterectomy or continence surgery increases the risk of developing voiding dysfunction (Haylen, 2007). The causes of female voiding dysfunction can be broadly categorized into detrusor underactivity and bladder outlet obstruction (BOO). These may have physiological, neurogenic, or iatrogenic origins. Detrusor underactivity is defined as a contraction of reduced strength and/or duration, leading to prolonged bladder emptying or incomplete emptying within a normal time span. BOO is characterized by physical obstruction during voiding, resulting in increased detrusor pressure and reduced urine flow rate (Abrams, 2003). Physiological causes of BOO include urogenital prolapse, urethral stricture, or obstruction. Iatrogenic causes may involve urethral trauma, surgery for continence or prolapse, or both (Robinson, 2012). Neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis or spinal cord compression can also present with altered voiding symptoms (Olujide, 2005). Urinary disturbances and voiding symptoms are frequently observed in individuals with Parkinson's disease, significantly affecting their quality of life (Yeo, 2012). Patients with voiding dysfunction should undergo a thorough evaluation, including urine analysis, uroflowmetry, and post-void residual urine measurement. If the free flow rate is abnormally low, filling cystometry with pressure-flow studies can help differentiate between detrusor underactivity and BOO. Urethral pressure profilometry may aid in diagnosing urethral stenosis or obstruction if BOO is suspected. Videocystourethrography can provide additional insights into lower urinary tract function and anatomy, particularly in cases of voiding difficulties following continence or pelvic surgery or when a neurogenic cause is suspected (Robinson, 2012). LUTS are categorized into storage, voiding, and post-micturition symptoms. This review focuses on voiding symptoms, which are distinct from storage symptoms. Voiding symptoms include hesitancy (delay in initiating urination), slow urinary stream, intermittent stream, splitting or spraying of the urinary stream, straining to void, terminal dribbling, position-dependent micturition (requiring specific positions to void), urinary retention, and dysuria. Post-micturition symptoms include a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying, the need to immediately re-void, and post-micturition dribbling.
